messages:
liz: Heads-up — after the kernel-picker change that prefers warp-specialized kernels by default, we see a 12-18% throughput regression on A10 for seq_len >= 2048. Observed increased tail latency too.
cheng: Ugh. Which kernel variant got chosen for those traces? did the picker pick v3-special or a fallback path? @dave can you look at the trace? :thinking:
dave: It picked WarpSpecTile_v3 for most long requests, then some fell back to GenericTile_v2 under burst. I dumped a short perf sample:
```
# top hotspots (A10, seq=2048, batch=4)
WarpSpecTile_v3          38.6%  (regs=72, spills=24)
GenericTile_v2           26.1%  (regs=56, spills=8)
KVCacheHandler           12.4%  (mem-wait)
Other kernels            23%
```
liz: That matches what I saw — high register pressure on v3 causing spills and slower SMEM prefetching. Also noticed increased L1 bank conflict rate when tile_size=64 on this path.
kevin: Do we have the kernel-picker heuristic code that decided on v3? last change introduced an architecture-aware bias to prefer warp-specialized on Hopper/A10. Maybe bias too strong for long-seq distributions.
cheng: Can you paste the snippet? I want to check the gating logic (seq_threshold vs occupancy).
dave: Here is the simplified logic we merged:
```
if (arch >= A10 && seq_len >= config.seq_cutoff && occupancy_estimate > 0.6) {
  prefer = WarpSpec
} else {
  prefer = Generic
}
```
liz: The problem seems to be occupancy_estimate calculation — it's using peak occupancy at small tile sizes, which overestimates for long KV paths. For long sequences, KV cache prefetch inflates regs+smem usage at runtime and occupancy drops, so v3 ends up underperforming.
cheng: Two quick mitigations: 1) lower the architecture bias weight for A10 when seq_len > 1024; 2) add a runtime fallback that monitors reg spill rate and flips to GenericTile if spills > threshold for N requests.
kevin: I like (2). We can instrument the runtime to count spills in the kernel planner and attach a short windowed metric. If spill_ratio > 0.06 for 20 requests -> route to generic. Low risk and immediate.
opsbot: @opsbot note: created ticket INF-2318 for "runtime fallback for high reg spill" (link: https://redwood.internal/t/INF-2318) :white_check_mark:
liz: Also found a KV-cache interaction: when warp-specialized does aggressive prefetch (prefetch_depth=4) it floods sharedmem banks and causes higher L1 miss latency on concurrent batches. Reducing prefetch_depth to 2 for long sequences reduces stalls.
cheng: So combined plan: add runtime spill-detection fallback, temporarily reduce A10 bias for seq > 1024, and set prefetch_depth=2 for warp-specialized long path. Can we roll a canary?
dave: I'll prepare a canary config for dedicated nodes: canary group = a10-longseq, 5% traffic for seq >= 1536, with fallback enabled. I'll push a build with metrics export for spill_ratio and bank-conflict rate.
kevin: When can we have the metric dashboard? need quick visibility to rollback.
dave: Can have dashboard in ~2 hours with existing metric templates (cpu/gpu device counters + custom spill_ratio).
opsbot: @opsbot deploy: canary build pushed to staging for a10-longseq. CI passed.
liz: Nice. One more note: there was a perf regression on microbatching heuristics too — warp-specialized assumes full batches; with microbatching it triggers less efficient tiling. We should add a microbatch-aware gating flag.
cheng: Agreed. Let's put that in follow-up after the canary stabilizes. For now focus on spill-fallback + prefetch depth + bias tweak.
kevin: I'll draft the change and PR description (include perf sample and canary plan). Assign to @dave for rollout.
liz: Thanks — ping me if you need sample traces. I'll attach a flamegraph and a condensed pprof after the canary lands. :thumbsup:
